subject: Science
board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Biology (4BI1) and Science (Double Award) (4SD0)
source: Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Biology 4BI1 / Double Award 4SD0 specification

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Practical: food tests and the energy in food
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you prove what is in a biscuit, and how much energy it holds, without tasting it?
objectives: Carry out and interpret the tests for glucose, starch, protein and fat
Describe the practical to find the energy content of a food sample (Higher/Paper 2 only)
Calculate energy per gram from a temperature rise
successCriteria: All: state the reagent and positive colour for each of the four food tests
Most: plan a safe, fair test and explain a result
Some: calculate energy per gram and evaluate the error (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: colour changes and specific heat capacity; Maths: rearranging equations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude (shukr) for provision and care in what we eat

keywords.def: a sugar such as glucose that gives a colour change with Benedict's solution
blue solution that turns purple or lilac with protein
ethanol then water: a cloudy white layer shows lipid (fat)
measuring energy released by burning a fuel or food using the heating of water

starter: Name the elements in a carbohydrate and in a protein.
Name the basic units that make up a protein.
What does an iodine solution look like at the start?

teach.heading: Four tests, four results
bullets: Test each sample in a clean tube
Record start and end colours
Heat only the Benedict's tube, in a water bath
teach.note: Display the table and let pupils cover the right-hand column and recall it. Benedict's needs a hot water bath (about 80 degrees C), not direct flame. Goggles on for all four tests.

head: Nutrient
Reagent
Method
Positive result
rows: Blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red
Shake with ethanol, pour into water

teach.heading: Model: interpret a set of results
bullets: Use the colour to judge what is present
More colour change means more sugar
Always compare with a negative control
teach.note: Talk through each step aloud. Stress that Benedict's gives a semi-quantitative idea only (green means a little, brick-red a lot).

model.problem: A food extract turns brick-red with Benedict's, blue-black with iodine and stays blue with biuret. The ethanol test gives a clear solution. What does it contain?
steps: Brick-red Benedict's means a lot of reducing sugar such as glucose
Blue-black iodine means starch is present
Biuret stayed blue so there is no protein
A clear ethanol test means no fat
model.answer: Glucose and starch present; no protein and no fat

teach.heading: Check: choose the test
bullets: Pick the test and the result
Show me on your whiteboards
teach.note: Hinge question. Most pupils choose the iodine option; discuss why heating is wrong for it.

check.q: A student adds iodine solution to a potato extract. Which result shows starch is present?
check.why: Iodine turns blue-black with starch. Brick-red is Benedict's with a lot of glucose, purple is biuret with protein, and a cloudy white layer is the lipid emulsion test.

teach.heading: Energy content of food (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Burn a weighed sample under a boiling tube of water
Measure the water temperature before and after
Energy = water mass x 4.2 x temperature rise
Divide by food mass for energy per gram
teach.note: Flag clearly: this point is Higher/Paper 2 only. Specific heat capacity of water is 4.2 J per g per degree C. 1 cm3 of water has a mass of 1 g. Safety: tie back hair, keep nuts away from anyone with allergies, use tongs or a mounted needle.

teach.heading: Model: calculate energy per gram (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Mass of water: 20 g
Temperature rise: 18 degrees C
Mass of food burned: 0.50 g
teach.note: Do the three-line calculation on the board; then ask why the real value in a data book is higher.

model.problem: 20 g of water is heated by 18 degrees C when 0.50 g of a nut burns. Calculate the energy released per gram of nut (4.2 J per g per degree C).
steps: Energy to water = 20 x 4.2 x 18 = 1512 J
Energy per gram = 1512 / 0.50 = 3024 J per g
Convert: 3024 J per g = about 3.0 kJ per g
model.answer: About 3.0 kJ per g (3024 J per g)

teach.heading: Why is the answer too low?
bullets: Heat escapes into the air
Food may burn incompletely
Some energy heats the tube and stand
teach.note: Improvements: draught shield or foil, put the tube close to the flame, stir the water, insulate. Ask pupils to say which fix tackles which loss.

misconception.wrong: The temperature rise measures all the energy in the food
misconception.right: Only part of the energy reaches the water, so the result underestimates the true value

practice: State the positive result for the biuret test.
A sample gives no colour change with Benedict's after heating. What does this tell you?
Higher: 25 g of water rises by 12 degrees C when 0.75 g of food burns. Calculate energy per gram.
independent: Core: Complete a results table of the four tests for milk, bread, egg white and oil with predictions.
Extend: Write a method to find which of three crisps has the most energy, listing control variables.
Stretch (Higher/Paper 2 only): Evaluate the energy practical and suggest two improvements, explaining the effect on the result.
exit: Which reagent tests for starch?
Why must the Benedict's tube be heated?
Why is energy measured by burning always an underestimate?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Describe how you would test a food sample for protein and for glucose.' (4 marks). Write a full answer with colour changes.
lessons.send: Support: table with reagent and colour pre-filled for matching. EAL: colour-coded vocabulary cards. Stretch: link to the energy value labels on food packaging.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: A balanced diet: nutrients, sources and energy needs
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do a pregnant mother, a teenage athlete and a grandfather need different plates?
objectives: Describe a balanced diet
State sources and functions of vitamins A, C and D, calcium, iron, water and fibre
Explain how energy needs vary with activity, age and pregnancy
successCriteria: All: list the seven components of a balanced diet
Most: give a source and function of each named nutrient and a deficiency
Some: explain energy requirement differences using data
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: healthy eating; Maths: reading bar charts of daily energy needs
lessons.smsc: Moral: eating in moderation and sharing food with those in need

keywords.def: contains all seven nutrient groups in the right proportions for the person's needs
a disease or condition caused by too little of a nutrient
indigestible plant material that keeps food moving through the gut
the energy a person needs each day to stay healthy

starter: Name the enzyme that digests starch and its product.
Which test shows protein is present?
What is the function of lipids as stored energy?

teach.heading: The seven components
bullets: Carbohydrate, protein, lipid
Vitamins and minerals
Water and fibre
Proportion matters: more carbohydrate than lipid
teach.note: Ask pupils to name a food that is a good source of each. The word 'balanced' means the right amounts for that person, not equal amounts.

teach.heading: Vitamins and minerals you must know
bullets: Vitamin A: healthy vision
Vitamin C: skin, gums and blood vessels
Vitamin D: calcium absorption
Calcium: bones and teeth
Iron: haemoglobin
teach.note: Link each to its deficiency: A (night blindness), C (scurvy), D (rickets), calcium (weak bones and teeth), iron (anaemia). Vitamin D can be made in skin in sunlight, so it is also in oily fish, eggs and fortified foods.

teach.heading: Check: link nutrient to job
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Most will choose iron correctly; the vitamin D option is the common trap.

check.q: A girl is tired and pale and has a low red blood cell count. Which nutrient is she most likely to be short of?
check.why: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, so a shortage causes anaemia. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, vitamin D deficiency rickets, and low fibre causes constipation.

teach.heading: Energy requirements vary
bullets: More activity needs more energy
Growing teenagers need a lot
Pregnancy needs extra energy and nutrients
Older adults are less active, so need less
teach.note: Give the idea, not memorised numbers. A very active person such as a builder or athlete needs more energy than someone at a desk. Adults over about 60 usually need less energy as metabolic rate and activity fall (approx.). A pregnant woman needs extra energy, protein, iron and calcium for the baby.

teach.heading: Model: explain a difference
bullets: Compare two people in a table
State the factor, then the reason
teach.note: Model the structure: factor, then because...

model.problem: A 15-year-old footballer needs more energy per day than a 70-year-old retired teacher. Explain why.
steps: The footballer is very active, so muscles respire faster and use more energy
He is still growing, so energy is needed to build new tissue
The older person is less active and no longer growing
model.answer: Higher activity level and growth give the footballer a greater energy requirement

teach.heading: Misconception: fibre and water
bullets: Fibre has no value because it is not digested
Water does not count as a nutrient
teach.note: Both are needed.

misconception.wrong: Fibre is useless because we cannot digest it
misconception.right: Fibre adds bulk so muscles can push food along by peristalsis and prevents constipation

practice: Name two functions of water in the body.
Which vitamin helps absorb calcium?
Give a food source of iron.
independent: Core: Plan a day's meals for a 14-year-old that includes all seven components, labelling each.
Extend: Explain the energy needs of a pregnant woman compared with a non-pregnant woman.
Stretch: A diet has plenty of calcium but no vitamin D. Explain what happens to the bones.
exit: Give the source and function of vitamin C.
Name three factors that change energy requirements.
What is meant by a balanced diet?
lessons.homework: Make a poster linking five nutrients to source, function and deficiency disease, and take a photo to share.
lessons.send: Support: sentence starters 'This nutrient is needed for...'. EAL: picture-based food cards. Stretch: compare dietary needs of a pupil fasting in Ramadan with a normal day (outside spec, discussion).

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Digestive enzymes and bile
lessons.bigQuestion: How does your body turn a chicken sandwich into molecules small enough to enter your blood?
objectives: Name the digestive enzymes, what they digest and the products
State where bile is made and stored
Explain how bile neutralises acid and emulsifies lipids
successCriteria: All: match each enzyme to its substrate
Most: state the products and where each enzyme is made
Some: explain why bile helps lipase and why the pH change matters
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: acids, alkalis and pH; Maths: surface area
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the precision of the body

keywords.def: enzyme that digests starch into maltose
enzyme that digests maltose into glucose
enzyme that digests protein into amino acids
enzyme that digests lipids into fatty acids and glycerol
breaking large fat droplets into tiny droplets to increase surface area

starter: What does pH measure?
What happens to an enzyme at a very high temperature?
Name the organ that churns food and mixes it with acid.

teach.heading: Enzymes of the gut
bullets: Amylase: starch to maltose
Maltase: maltose to glucose
Protease: protein to amino acids
Lipase: lipid to fatty acids and glycerol
teach.note: Remind pupils that enzymes are specific: one enzyme fits one substrate. Amylase is made in the salivary glands and pancreas; maltase is on the lining of the small intestine; proteases such as pepsin work in the stomach and others in the small intestine; lipase comes from the pancreas.

teach.heading: Bile: made, stored, released
bullets: Made in the liver
Stored in the gall bladder
Released into the small intestine
Contains no enzymes
teach.note: Trace bile on a diagram: liver, gall bladder, bile duct, duodenum. Many pupils think bile digests fat chemically; it does not, it only prepares the fat.

teach.heading: What bile does
bullets: Alkaline: neutralises stomach acid
Gives suitable pH for intestinal enzymes
Emulsifies lipids into tiny droplets
Larger surface area for lipase
teach.note: Link to enzyme work: the stomach acid is about pH 2 which would denature the intestinal enzymes. Emulsification is physical, not chemical.

left.title: Neutralising acid
points: Raises pH from the stomach's acid
Enzymes in intestine work best at alkaline pH

right.title: Emulsifying lipids
points: Large droplets split into small ones

teach.heading: Model: explain a data point
bullets: Identify the process
Link to surface area or pH
teach.note: Walk through the three-part answer.

model.problem: Explain why lipids are digested faster in the small intestine when bile is present.
steps: Bile emulsifies lipids, breaking large droplets into many small droplets
This increases the surface area of lipid available
Lipase can act on more lipid at once, so digestion is faster
model.answer: Emulsification increases the surface area for lipase to work on

teach.heading: Check: what does bile do?
bullets: Pick the best answer
teach.note: The common wrong choice is digesting fat chemically.

check.q: Which statement about bile is correct?
options: It is made in the gall bladder and digests lipids
It is made in the liver and emulsifies lipids
It is made in the pancreas and neutralises acid
It is an enzyme that breaks down fats
check.why: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder, and it emulsifies lipids and neutralises acid. It is not an enzyme and it is not made in the pancreas.

practice: Name the product of protease digestion.
Where is maltase found?
Why must the stomach acid be neutralised in the small intestine?
independent: Core: Complete a table of the four enzymes, substrates, products.
Extend: Explain why bile does not digest lipids even though it helps their digestion.
Stretch: Predict what would happen to digestion after the bile duct is blocked by a gallstone.
exit: Where is bile stored?
Give two functions of bile.
Name the enzyme that digests starch.
lessons.homework: Draw and label the digestive system showing where each enzyme is made, with one line on each.
lessons.send: Support: colour-matching enzyme cards. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: explain why fat-rich foods can cause discomfort after gall bladder removal.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Moving substances and the limits of size
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can an amoeba get by on diffusion alone but an elephant cannot?
objectives: Describe diffusion, osmosis and active transport in and out of cells
Explain how SA:V ratio, distance, temperature and concentration gradient affect the rate
Explain why unicellular organisms can rely on diffusion
successCriteria: All: define the three processes
Most: calculate a surface area to volume ratio and explain rate factors
Some: explain why multicellular organisms need a transport system
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: ratio and surface area; Chemistry: particles and kinetic energy
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at the tiny scale of life

keywords.def: the surface area of an object divided by its volume
the difference in concentration between two regions
made of a single cell
how far particles must travel

starter: Define diffusion.
Which process needs energy from respiration?
State the formula for percentage change.

teach.heading: Three processes into and out of cells
bullets: Diffusion: high to low, no energy
Osmosis: water through a partially permeable membrane
Active transport: low to high, uses energy
teach.note: Review quickly, then set up the rate factors. Examples: oxygen diffusing into cells; water into root hair cells by osmosis; mineral ions into root hairs by active transport; glucose absorption in the gut can use active transport.

teach.heading: What controls the rate?
bullets: Bigger surface area to volume ratio: faster
Shorter diffusion distance: faster
Higher temperature: faster
Steeper concentration gradient: faster
teach.note: For temperature say that particles have more kinetic energy and move faster. For active transport the rate also depends on respiration, so oxygen and temperature matter too.

teach.heading: Model: surface area to volume ratio
bullets: Cube of side 1 cm and side 2 cm
Find SA, then V, then divide
teach.note: Write both cubes on the board.

model.problem: Compare the SA:V ratio of a 1 cm cube with a 2 cm cube.
steps: 1 cm cube: SA = 6 x 1 x 1 = 6 cm2; V = 1 cm3; ratio = 6 : 1
2 cm cube: SA = 6 x 2 x 2 = 24 cm2; V = 8 cm3; ratio = 3 : 1
The smaller cube has the larger ratio
model.answer: 6 : 1 and 3 : 1: smaller objects have the larger SA:V ratio

teach.heading: Single cells and large bodies
bullets: Amoeba: large SA:V, short distance
Diffusion is quick enough for its needs
Large animals have small SA:V and long distances
They need a transport system
teach.note: Contrast an amoeba with a mammal. Large organisms also have specialised gas exchange surfaces and circulatory systems.

teach.heading: Check: the rate
bullets: One answer only
teach.note: Rule out the distractors using each factor in turn.

check.q: Which change would make diffusion of oxygen into a cell slower?
options: Reduce the oxygen concentration outside the cell
Increase the surface area of the cell
check.why: A lower outside concentration reduces the concentration gradient so diffusion is slower. The other three changes all increase the rate.

practice: Calculate the SA:V ratio of a 3 cm cube.
Give one example of active transport.
Why does a thin membrane increase the rate of diffusion?
independent: Core: Complete a table of SA:V for cubes with sides 1, 2, 3 and 4 cm and describe the trend.
Extend: Explain why a flat worm can survive without a circulatory system but a mouse cannot.
Stretch: Explain why a drop in oxygen reduces the rate of active transport in root hair cells.
exit: State three factors that affect the rate of diffusion.
Why can an amoeba rely on diffusion?
What is a concentration gradient?
lessons.homework: Practice questions: calculate the SA:V ratio of three different blocks and explain which would exchange substances fastest.
lessons.send: Support: foam blocks or sugar cubes for visual SA:V. EAL: glossary with diagrams. Stretch: introduce the idea that cube ratios scale as 6 divided by side length.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Photosynthesis practicals and net gas exchange
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you prove that a leaf needs light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll to make food?
objectives: Describe practicals that show oxygen is evolved and starch is made
Explain the need for light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll
Explain how net gas exchange depends on light intensity (Higher/Paper 2 only)
successCriteria: All: describe the starch test on a leaf
Most: interpret results of leaf experiments with foil and variegated leaves
Some: predict net gas exchange at different light intensities (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: solvents and flammability; Maths: interpreting graphs
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: signs in plants that sustain all life

keywords.def: leaving a plant in the dark so it uses up its starch
a leaf with green and white areas
the overall exchange of gases after photosynthesis and respiration
the light intensity at which photosynthesis and respiration rates are equal

starter: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
Name the pigment that absorbs light.
State one limiting factor of photosynthesis.

teach.heading: Testing a leaf for starch
bullets: Boil the leaf in water
Warm it in ethanol in a water bath
Rinse in water
Add iodine solution: blue-black means starch
teach.note: Explain each step: boiling kills the cells and softens the leaf; ethanol removes chlorophyll so the colour change is visible; ethanol is flammable, so no naked flame, use a hot water bath. Starch is the stored product of photosynthesis.

teach.heading: Showing each requirement
bullets: Light: cover part of a leaf with foil
Carbon dioxide: use soda lime in a sealed bell jar
Chlorophyll: use a variegated leaf
Destarch the plant in the dark first
teach.note: Controls matter: a control plant with carbon dioxide and a fully exposed leaf. Results: starch only in uncovered green parts with carbon dioxide.

teach.heading: Model: interpret a variegated leaf
bullets: Look at the colour pattern
Match starch to chlorophyll
teach.note: Ask pupils to sketch the expected result before showing it.

model.problem: A destarched variegated leaf is placed in light for a day and then tested with iodine. Only the green parts turn blue-black. What does this show?
steps: Blue-black means starch is present in the green parts
The white parts have no chlorophyll and no starch
So chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis

teach.heading: Oxygen evolution (pondweed)
bullets: Count bubbles or collect gas volume
Change light distance and record rate
Use a heat shield or water bath for temperature
teach.note: Test the gas with a glowing splint if collected. The distance from lamp is a way to change light intensity. Practical issues: bubble size varies, so measure volume if possible.

teach.heading: Net gas exchange (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Plants respire all the time, day and night
In the dark only respiration: CO2 out, O2 in
In bright light photosynthesis exceeds respiration
Net: CO2 taken in, O2 released
teach.note: Mark as Higher/Paper 2 only. Hydrogen-carbonate indicator: red at normal CO2, yellow when CO2 increases, purple when it decreases. At the compensation point there is no net change.

teach.heading: Check: net gas exchange (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Choose your answer
teach.note: The trap is the idea that plants only respire at night.

check.q: A leaf in a tube with hydrogen-carbonate indicator turns yellow. What explains this?
options: The leaf is absorbing carbon dioxide
check.why: Yellow means carbon dioxide has increased, so the leaf is releasing more carbon dioxide by respiration than it takes in by photosynthesis, as in the dark.

practice: State why the leaf is boiled in ethanol.
What would you expect under a foil strip? Explain.
Define net gas exchange.
independent: Core: Write a method to show that light is needed for photosynthesis including destarching.
Extend: Explain the results from a leaf where the CO2 was removed.
Stretch (Higher/Paper 2 only): Sketch how net CO2 exchange changes from darkness to bright light and mark the compensation point.
exit: Which colour shows starch with iodine?
Why is the plant destarched?
What does yellow indicator show?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Describe an experiment to show that chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.' (5 marks).
lessons.send: Support: step cards to sequence the starch test. EAL: bilingual keywords. Stretch: explain why the compensation point rises with higher temperature.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Transpiration and the environment (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a washing line dry faster on a windy day, and what has that got to do with a tree?
objectives: Describe the effect of humidity, wind speed, temperature and light intensity on transpiration rate
Explain each effect using evaporation and diffusion
Interpret potometer data
successCriteria: All: name the four factors and say whether each increases or decreases the rate
Most: explain each using the concentration gradient
Some: calculate transpiration rate from potometer measurements
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: volume of a cylinder; Geography: weather and climate
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: observing the water cycle in a single tree

keywords.def: loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata
the amount of water vapour in the air
apparatus that measures water uptake by a shoot
pores in the leaf surface that open and close

starter: Define transpiration.
Which tissue carries water up the plant?
What do guard cells control?

teach.heading: Four factors (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Light intensity up: rate up
Temperature up: rate up
Wind speed up: rate up
Humidity up: rate down
teach.note: State that these are Higher/Paper 2 only. Light opens the stomata; warm air increases evaporation and gives molecules more energy; wind removes water vapour from near the leaf; high humidity reduces the concentration gradient.

teach.heading: The concentration gradient idea
bullets: Inside the leaf the air is humid
Outside the air is drier
Vapour diffuses out through open stomata
teach.note: Draw a leaf section and show the gradient. Stress that a smaller gradient means slower diffusion.

teach.heading: Model: use a potometer
bullets: Measure bubble movement
Use volume of a cylinder: pi x r2 x length
teach.note: Choose a capillary radius of 0.5 mm. It is an estimate of transpiration because the shoot uses a little water.

model.problem: In a potometer the bubble moves 36 mm in 6 minutes. The capillary radius is 0.5 mm. Find the rate of water uptake in mm3 per minute.
steps: Volume = pi x 0.5 x 0.5 x 36 = about 28.3 mm3
= about 4.7 mm3 per minute

teach.heading: Check: predict the effect
bullets: Choose one
teach.note: Discuss why high humidity is the odd one out.

check.q: Which condition gives the fastest transpiration rate?
check.why: Warm, windy, dry and bright conditions each increase transpiration: faster evaporation, humid air removed, steeper gradient and open stomata.

teach.heading: Misconception: wind and temperature
bullets: Transpiration only happens in hot weather
teach.note: Plants transpire day and night but fastest in warm, dry, windy, bright conditions.

misconception.wrong: Wind cools the leaf so transpiration slows down
misconception.right: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the gradient steep, so transpiration speeds up

practice: State two factors that increase transpiration.
Why does high humidity reduce the rate?
What is the function of guard cells?
independent: Core: Complete a table of the four factors, direction of change and reason.
Extend: Predict and explain the result of a hair dryer on a shoot in a potometer.
Stretch: Calculate transpiration rate from a bubble that moves 24 mm in 4 minutes in a 1.0 mm radius capillary.
exit: How does wind increase transpiration?
Why does light matter?
What does a potometer measure?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Explain why the rate of transpiration is higher on a warm, windy day than on a cool, calm day.' (4 marks).
lessons.send: Support: diagram with arrows to label the gradient. EAL: key words matched to pictures. Stretch: wilting and why a plant may close stomata on a hot day.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Blood: plasma, red cells and platelets
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is a red blood cell shaped like a doughnut with a dent instead of a hole?
objectives: State what plasma transports
Explain how red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen
Describe how platelets cause blood clotting (Higher/Paper 2 only)
successCriteria: All: list the substances carried in plasma
Most: explain three red blood cell adaptations
Some: describe the clotting process and why it matters (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: reversible reactions; PSHE: first aid for bleeding
lessons.smsc: Moral: donating blood and helping others (sadaqah) as a medical act of care

keywords.def: the pale yellow liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances
red protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen
curved inwards on both sides, like a disc with a dip
small cell fragments that help blood to clot

starter: Name the four components of blood.
What does a phagocyte do?
State the function of the nucleus.

teach.heading: What plasma carries
bullets: Carbon dioxide from tissues to lungs
Digested food such as glucose and amino acids
Urea from the liver to the kidneys
Hormones and heat around the body
teach.note: Plasma is about 90 per cent water (approx.), with dissolved substances. Heat is spread from active organs such as muscles and liver to the rest of the body. Do not confuse plasma with serum or with blood as a whole.

teach.heading: Red blood cells: built for oxygen
bullets: Biconcave disc: large surface area to volume ratio
No nucleus: more room for haemoglobin
Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs
Releases it in respiring tissues
teach.note: Link back to SA:V and diffusion. Haemoglobin plus oxygen makes oxyhaemoglobin in the lungs where oxygen is plentiful; it releases oxygen where oxygen is low. The flexible shape helps them squeeze through capillaries.

teach.heading: Model: explain an adaptation
bullets: Feature, then function, then reason
teach.note: Model the three-part structure.

model.problem: Explain how the absence of a nucleus helps a red blood cell carry oxygen.
steps: Red blood cells have no nucleus
This leaves more space inside the cell
More haemoglobin can be packed in, so more oxygen is carried
model.answer: No nucleus means more room for haemoglobin, so more oxygen is transported

teach.heading: Platelets and clotting (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Platelets are cell fragments
At a wound they help form a clot
A fibrin mesh traps blood cells to form a scab
Stops blood loss and blocks microbes
teach.note: Flag: Higher/Paper 2 only. Fibrinogen (soluble) becomes fibrin (insoluble threads) when platelets and clotting factors are activated. The scab protects until new skin grows. Haemophilia is an inherited failure of clotting (extension).

teach.heading: Check: plasma and red cells
bullets: Select the correct pair
teach.note: The trap is oxygen being carried in plasma.

check.q: Which substance is carried mainly by red blood cells rather than plasma?
check.why: Most oxygen is bound to haemoglobin inside red blood cells. Urea, glucose and hormones are dissolved in plasma.

practice: Name three things carried by plasma.
Why are red blood cells biconcave?
Higher: What are platelets?
independent: Core: Draw and annotate a red blood cell with three adaptations.
Extend: Explain why a person living at high altitude may make more red blood cells.
Stretch (Higher/Paper 2 only): Explain why clotting is important and what might happen if platelets are missing.
exit: State the function of haemoglobin.
What does plasma carry from the liver to the kidneys?
Higher: Name the protein mesh of a clot.
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph linking the structure and function of a red blood cell and plasma.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagram to complete. EAL: bilingual word cards. Stretch: relate carbon monoxide poisoning to haemoglobin.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Heart rate, exercise and adrenaline
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does your heart pound when you run, and again when you are frightened?
objectives: Explain why heart rate rises during exercise
Describe the effect of adrenaline on the heart
Interpret heart rate data and recovery time
successCriteria: All: state that heart rate increases during exercise and with adrenaline
Most: explain why using oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide
Some: analyse recovery data and calculate percentage change
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentage change and graphs; PE: fitness and recovery
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awareness of the body as an amanah (trust)

keywords.def: hormone from the adrenal glands that prepares the body for action
the number of heartbeats per minute
time for heart rate to return to resting level after exercise
the pressure wave in an artery caused by each heartbeat

starter: Name the four chambers of the heart.
Which gas is a waste product of respiration?
What is a hormone?

teach.heading: Heart rate in exercise
bullets: Muscles respire faster
They need more oxygen and glucose
Carbon dioxide level in blood rises
Brain raises heart rate, so blood flows faster
teach.note: The brain detects the higher carbon dioxide level and signals the heart to beat faster. Faster blood flow supplies oxygen and glucose and removes carbon dioxide and heat.

teach.heading: Adrenaline
bullets: Made by the adrenal glands
Released in danger or excitement
Acts on the heart: beats faster and harder
Prepares for fight or flight
teach.note: Adrenaline travels in the blood plasma; it is a hormone so it acts more slowly than nerves but lasts longer. It also widens the pupils and raises blood glucose; blood is diverted to muscles. Connect to existing hormone lessons.

teach.heading: Model: percentage increase
bullets: Use (new - old) / old x 100
teach.note: Show the calculation line by line.

model.problem: A student's heart rate rises from 70 beats per minute at rest to 150 beats per minute after running. Find the percentage increase.
steps: Increase = 150 - 70 = 80
x 100 = 114 per cent (to nearest whole number)

teach.heading: Reading recovery data
bullets: Fitter people recover faster
Recovery time = minutes to return to resting rate
Compare using the same exercise
teach.note: Present a table of two students; pupils compare recovery and suggest why. Keep to data, not claims about fitness levels.

teach.heading: Check: why does it rise?
bullets: Choose the best explanation
teach.note: The distractors mix up cause and effect.

check.q: What is the main reason heart rate increases during exercise?
options: To deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles and remove carbon dioxide
To increase the volume of blood
check.why: Active muscles need more oxygen and glucose for respiration and produce more carbon dioxide, so blood must flow faster.

practice: Name the gland that makes adrenaline.
Calculate the percentage increase from 60 to 135 beats per minute.
Why does faster blood flow help muscles?
independent: Core: Plot a graph of heart rate before, during and after exercise from given data and describe it.
Extend: Explain why a fitter person has a shorter recovery time.
Stretch: Explain why adrenaline has an effect on the heart in addition to the nervous system.
exit: State two effects of adrenaline.
Why does heart rate rise in exercise?
What is recovery time?
lessons.homework: Measure your pulse at rest and after one minute of star jumps (if safe), record and calculate the percentage change.
lessons.send: Support: calculation frame. EAL: sentence starters. Stretch: heart rate and stroke volume (extension, outside the spec).

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: The urinary system and the nephron (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a pair of organs the size of your fist clean all of your blood?
objectives: Name and locate the parts of the urinary system
Describe the structure of a nephron
Link each part of the nephron to its function
successCriteria: All: name kidney, ureter, bladder and urethra and their jobs
Most: label the nephron
Some: explain how structure suits function
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: solutions; PSHE: health and hydration
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the body, as a trust

keywords.def: tube carrying urine from kidney to bladder
tube carrying urine out of the body from the bladder
microscopic filtering unit of the kidney
knot of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule

starter: Name two excretory organs.
What is urea and where is it made?
Define excretion.

teach.heading: The urinary system (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Kidneys filter blood, make urine
Ureters carry urine to the bladder
Bladder stores urine
Urethra releases urine
teach.note: Flag: Higher/Paper 2 only. Renal artery brings blood to the kidney and the renal vein takes cleaned blood away. Ask pupils to trace a drop of urine through the system.

teach.heading: Inside the kidney: the nephron
bullets: Bowman's capsule surrounds glomerulus
Proximal convoluted tubule
Loop of Henle
Distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct
teach.note: Each kidney has about a million nephrons (approx.). Sketch the nephron in order and let pupils copy.

head: Part
What it is
Role
rows: Carries urine to ureter; water reabsorbed

teach.heading: Model: trace the filtrate
bullets: Name the part, then say what happens
teach.note: Tell the story in order from the capsule outwards.

model.problem: Describe the path taken by a molecule of urea from the blood to the urethra.
steps: Filtered out of the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule
Flows along the tubule, loop of Henle and collecting duct
Leaves the kidney in the ureter, is stored in the bladder and passes out through the urethra
model.answer: Glomerulus, capsule, tubule, collecting duct, ureter, bladder, urethra

teach.heading: Check: identify the part
bullets: One answer
teach.note: Common error: confusing ureter and urethra.

check.q: Which part of the nephron is the knot of capillaries where blood is filtered?
check.why: The glomerulus is the capillary knot. The Bowman's capsule is the cup around it, and the loop of Henle and collecting duct are tubules.

teach.heading: Misconception: ureter and urethra
bullets: They are the same tube
teach.note: Use memory trick: ureter = from kidney; urethra = out of the body.

misconception.wrong: The ureter carries urine out of the body
misconception.right: The ureters carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder; the urethra carries it out

practice: Name the organ that stores urine.
Where is the glomerulus found?
Why are there many nephrons in each kidney?
independent: Core: Label a nephron diagram and a urinary system diagram.
Extend: Explain how the structure of the glomerulus suits filtration.
Stretch: Compare the renal artery with the renal vein in terms of urea concentration.
exit: Name the tube that carries urine out of the body.
What is the Bowman's capsule?
Which part collects urine from many nephrons?
lessons.homework: Draw a flow chart showing the path of blood and urine through the kidney.
lessons.send: Support: pre-drawn outline with word bank. EAL: bilingual labels. Stretch: describe how the kidney can be replaced by dialysis.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: Ultrafiltration and reabsorption of glucose (Higher/Paper 2 only)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would a drop of sugar in your urine tell a doctor something is wrong?
objectives: Explain ultrafiltration in the Bowman's capsule
State the composition of glomerular filtrate
Explain selective reabsorption of glucose in the proximal convoluted tubule
successCriteria: All: state which substances are filtered and which are not
Most: explain why high pressure is needed
Some: explain why glucose appears in urine if blood glucose is very high
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: solutions and particle size; Maths: percentages
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: balance and precision in the body

keywords.def: filtration under high pressure forcing small molecules out of the blood
fluid in the Bowman's capsule containing small molecules from the blood
taking back useful substances into the blood from the filtrate
first coiled tubule after the Bowman's capsule

starter: What is the function of the glomerulus?
Describe active transport.
Name two substances found in urine.

teach.heading: Ultrafiltration (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Blood enters the glomerulus at high pressure
The efferent vessel is narrower than the afferent
Small molecules are forced into the capsule
Large molecules and cells stay in the blood
teach.note: Flag: Higher/Paper 2 only. Pressure builds because the vessel leaving the glomerulus is narrower than the one entering. Filtration is not selective by usefulness; it is by size.

teach.heading: Selective reabsorption
bullets: Happens in the proximal convoluted tubule
All glucose is reabsorbed
By active transport, using energy
Cells have many mitochondria and microvilli
teach.note: Link to active transport against the concentration gradient. Also amino acids, many ions and much water return to the blood; urea mostly stays. Microvilli increase surface area.

teach.heading: Model: explain glucose in urine
bullets: Use the idea of a limit on reabsorption
teach.note: Make explicit that carrier proteins can be saturated.

model.problem: A person with untreated diabetes has glucose in their urine. Explain why.
steps: Blood glucose is very high so a lot of glucose is filtered into the capsule
The carriers in the proximal tubule can only transport a limited amount
Extra glucose is not reabsorbed and passes out in urine
model.answer: The reabsorption mechanism is overwhelmed, so glucose stays in the urine

teach.heading: Model: how much is reabsorbed?
bullets: Typical figures (approx.): about 180 dm3 filtered per day
About 1.5 dm3 of urine passes out
teach.note: These are textbook approximations. The point is that almost all of the filtrate returns to the blood. Verify the figures against your textbook before quoting.

model.problem: About 180 dm3 of filtrate forms per day and about 1.5 dm3 of urine is produced (approx.). Estimate the percentage reabsorbed.
steps: Volume reabsorbed = 180 - 1.5 = 178.5 dm3
x 100 = about 99 per cent
model.answer: About 99 per cent of the filtrate is reabsorbed (approx.)

teach.heading: Check: glomerular filtrate
bullets: One answer
teach.note: Most common error: thinking blood proteins are filtered.

check.q: Which substance is NOT normally found in the glomerular filtrate?
check.why: Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the glomerulus. Glucose, urea and water are small enough to be filtered.

practice: Why is the blood pressure high in the glomerulus?
Where is glucose reabsorbed?
Name two substances in urine.
independent: Core: Complete a table of filtered, reabsorbed and excreted substances.
Extend: Explain why the proximal tubule cells contain many mitochondria.
Stretch: Compare the glucose concentration in the filtrate, the end of the proximal tubule and urine.
exit: What is ultrafiltration?
Which process reabsorbs glucose?
Why does glucose appear in urine in diabetes?
lessons.homework: Exam-style: 'Explain how the structure of the nephron allows it to filter blood and reabsorb glucose.' (6 marks).
lessons.send: Support: sorting cards for 'filtered' or 'stays in blood'. EAL: key terms in table. Stretch: link to kidney function tests (verify content).

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: The nervous system: CNS, impulses and synapses
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a signal cross a gap that is far narrower than a hair?
objectives: Describe the central nervous system and how it links to sense organs
Explain how receptors send electrical impulses along nerves
Describe how neurotransmitters transmit signals across synapses
successCriteria: All: name the parts of the CNS and give the role of nerves
Most: describe the order from stimulus to response
Some: explain why synapses make transmission one-way
lessons.crossCurricular: Physics: electrical signals; PE: reaction times
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at rapid, coordinated responses

keywords.def: the brain and spinal cord
a cell or organ that detects a stimulus
a nerve cell that carries electrical impulses
a gap between two neurones
chemical that diffuses across a synapse to pass on a signal

starter: Name the neurone that carries an impulse to a muscle.
What is a stimulus?
What are effectors?

teach.heading: Structure of the nervous system
bullets: CNS = brain and spinal cord
Nerves link sense organs to the CNS
Nerves link the CNS to muscles and glands
teach.note: Show the stimulus, receptor, coordinator, effector, response chain. Sense organs include eye, ear, skin, nose and tongue.

teach.heading: Electrical impulses
bullets: Receptors convert stimuli into impulses
Impulses travel along neurones
Response is rapid and short-lived
Effectors: muscles contract, glands secrete
teach.note: Compare with hormones, which travel in the blood. Impulses are electrical signals, not 'electricity' in the mains sense.

teach.heading: Synapses
bullets: A gap between neurones
Impulse reaches the end of neurone 1
Neurotransmitter is released and diffuses across
It binds receptors on neurone 2 and starts a new impulse
teach.note: Because only the first neurone releases neurotransmitter, the impulse goes one way. The delay is tiny.

teach.heading: Model: explain one-way transmission
bullets: Say who releases and who has receptors
teach.note: Spell out the logic carefully.

model.problem: Explain why an impulse travels in one direction across a synapse.
steps: Only the first neurone releases neurotransmitter into the gap
Only the second neurone has receptors for it
So the signal can only pass from the first to the second
model.answer: Neurotransmitter is released on one side only and the receptors are on the other side

teach.heading: Check: crossing the gap
bullets: One answer
teach.note: The trap is believing the electrical impulse jumps the gap.

check.q: How does a signal cross a synapse?
options: A hormone is released into the blood
check.why: A chemical, the neurotransmitter, diffuses across the gap and triggers a new impulse; the impulse itself does not cross.

practice: What is the CNS?
Give the role of a receptor.
Name the chemical that crosses a synapse.
independent: Core: Complete a flow diagram from stimulus to response for touching a hot pan.
Extend: Compare nervous and hormonal communication in a table.
Stretch: Explain why drugs that block neurotransmitter receptors can affect the nervous system.
exit: What carries information from the receptor?
What happens at a synapse?
State one difference between nerves and hormones.
lessons.homework: Make a labelled diagram of a synapse and write three sentences to explain it.
lessons.send: Support: sequencing cards for the synapse. EAL: bilingual vocabulary. Stretch: link to reaction time practical.

lessons.unit: Biology 2: Structure and functions in living organisms
lessons.title: The eye: focusing and light intensity
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can you see a distant mountain clearly and then read a book a moment later?
objectives: Explain how the eye focuses on near and distant objects
Describe how the iris controls light entry
Predict changes in the eye for a given situation
successCriteria: All: state that the lens changes shape to focus
Most: describe ciliary muscles and suspensory ligaments for near and far
Some: explain the pupil response and its purpose
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on sight as a gift

keywords.def: changing the shape of the lens to focus
ring of muscle that alters the shape of the lens
fibres attaching the lens to the ciliary muscle
coloured ring of muscle controlling pupil size

starter: Name the part of the eye where light is detected.
What does refraction mean?
What is a reflex?

teach.heading: Focusing on a near object
bullets: Ciliary muscles contract
Suspensory ligaments slacken
Lens becomes thicker and more curved
Light is refracted more
teach.note: Show the pairing: contract/slack/thick. Mnemonic: near = contract.

teach.heading: Model: explain focusing
bullets: Start with the muscle, end with refraction
teach.note: Practise the chain of reasoning aloud.

model.problem: Explain how the eye focuses on a book held close to the face.
steps: Ciliary muscles contract
Suspensory ligaments become slack
The lens is thicker and more curved
Light is refracted more strongly and focuses on the retina
model.answer: The lens becomes thicker so that light from the near object is focused on the retina

teach.heading: Light intensity and the pupil
bullets: Bright light: circular muscles contract
Radial muscles relax, pupil gets smaller
Dim light: radial muscles contract
Circular muscles relax, pupil gets larger
teach.note: The pupil reflex protects the retina from damage in bright light and lets in more light in dim conditions.

teach.heading: Check: pupil response
bullets: One answer
teach.note: Make sure pupils connect circular with constriction.

check.q: What happens to the eye when moving from a dark room into bright sunlight?
options: The pupil gets smaller as circular muscles contract
check.why: Circular muscles of the iris contract so the pupil constricts to protect the retina; the radial muscles relax.

teach.heading: Misconception: distant objects
bullets: The lens is thicker for distance
teach.note: Check understanding of the muscle-ligament relationship.

misconception.wrong: For a distant object the ciliary muscles contract
misconception.right: For a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the ligaments pull tight and the lens becomes thin

practice: Name the muscle controlling the pupil's size.
What happens to the lens for near vision?
Why does the pupil constrict in bright light?
independent: Core: Complete a table comparing near and far focusing.
Extend: Explain what happens to the lens as a person looks up from reading to a distant tree.
Stretch: Explain why older people often need reading glasses (lens less flexible, approx.).
exit: State how the pupil changes in dim light.
What do suspensory ligaments do?
Why does the lens change shape?
lessons.homework: Draw and annotate eye diagrams for near and distant vision and for bright and dim light.
lessons.send: Support: matching cards. EAL: bilingual labels. Stretch: link to eye defects (outside spec).
